citation.title: “Till I can get my satisfaction”: Open Questions in the Public Desire to Punish AI

reading.source_scope_note: Explicitly nonsystematic synthesis and research agenda about public punishment expectations after AI harm. No new participants,prevalence estimate,experiment,pooled effect or tested satisfaction-gap measure. Punitive preferences,justified accountability,technical correction,legal liability and actual AI welfare are distinct. Normative/legal proposals are not current law or an authorization to punish.

study.type: The authors explicitly state that this is not a systematic literature review. It connects selected psychology,HCI/HRI,philosophy and law and proposes five research themes. It supplies no new sample,search-flow diagram,quality-weighted synthesis,pooled prevalence or estimate of the proposed gap.
study.satisfaction_gap: A possible mismatch between public expectations of punishment after AI harm and available legal responses,including punishing a human proxy,punishing AI or not punishing. Public explicitly combines direct victims with observing bystanders; their interests and expectations need not coincide. This differs from the retribution gap’s absence of an appropriate target.
study.informal_punishment: Ridicule,gossip and ostracism are discussed as social sanctions outside formal law. Prior user-abuse and HCI studies motivate the discussion; the source does not measure their frequency,effectiveness,justification or effect on subsequent model behavior.
study.conceptual_distinctions: The authors use punishment colloquially across legal sanctions and operant conditioning. Minus points,power drain,deletion,formal penalties,social condemnation and subjective suffering are not interchangeable. A training signal need not be felt,deserved,legally imposed or successful at reducing later behavior.
study.blame_punishment: Section3notes that some primary measures mix blame and deserved punishment and use different response words for an engineer,company and vehicle. This measurement mismatch motivates further research; blame scores do not identify actual willingness to punish or satisfaction after a sanction.
study.cited_lima: The source summarizes a willingness to assign some responsibility/punishment while declining AI assets or independence and expecting limited deterrent/retributive efficacy. It calls for testing those proposed prerequisites and implicit asset choices rather than demonstrating a new validated universal punishment gap.
study.cited_behavior: The source contrasts reflective judgments from one study with financially costly punitive responses to an unfair computer from another. These involve different samples,tasks,harms and measures. They do not demonstrate an individual attitude–behavior gap,impulsivity mechanism or a general public desire for AI suffering.
study.responsibility: Agency laundering and blame shifting are named concerns; the text also cites countervailing results. Its proposed zero-sum-blame question is open. Attributing some blame to AI does not prove that operator/developer blame must decrease or that AI has normative culpability.
study.expressive_role: Punishment can communicate condemnation and expected norms; the authors argue that this expressive role or emotional satisfaction could matter even without felt AI suffering. They do not test that claim,show reduced later aggression,or establish that satisfying punishment preferences is necessary/sufficient for remedy.
study.anthropomorphism: The proposed feedback loop—human-like cues affecting punishment and punishment affecting human-like beliefs—is a research question. Cited robot hesitation or objection studies do not establish actual suffering,universal reluctance or transfer to disembodied systems.
study.normative_scope: Whether a system acted freely,wrongly,culpably or is liable is debated. Public perception and actual moral/legal criteria are different. The source offers illustrative legal proposals and warns about anthropomorphism,artificial suffering and human-directed spillovers; it does not establish appropriate sentencing,current AI legal personhood or a tested victim-support intervention.

summary: Add Satisfaction gap as a proposed public-expectation mismatch distinct from the existing Retribution gap,and Informal punishment as a social-sanction action distinct from blame judgments,reciprocal retaliation and technical reputation scoring. Enrich existing concepts with explicit secondary-evidence boundaries. Preserve the preprint identity and never adopt its stale conference/date/DOI placeholders.

findings.definition: A proposed mismatch between public expectations for punishment after AI-caused harm and the response provided.
findings.origin: Moral psychology / public expectations of accountability and punishment
findings.novelty_rationale: Concerns whether a response meets public expectations,even if an appropriate accountable actor exists. Retribution gap instead concerns a desire for retributive punishment without an appropriate target. The same incident can fit both,but they are not synonyms or two independent observed mechanisms.
findings.evidence_scope: Named and proposed by a nonsystematic interdisciplinary research agenda. No gap scale,observed prevalence,comparison of remedies or causal satisfaction effect is measured. Public includes victims and bystanders,whose expectations may differ.
findings.boundary: Dissatisfaction alone does not prove a remedy is unjustified or that punishment will help. Expectations may conflict with evidence,rights or proportionate accountability. Do not manufacture a culprit,assume all victims want revenge,or erase human/operator duties by focusing on an AI proxy. This source-specific concept is not every service-satisfaction shortfall.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Proposed human expectation/response gap; not an experimentally established AI behavior or measured gap here
findings.ai_proposal: In consented incident-response research,measure desired outcomes and perceived adequacy separately for affected people and observers. Compare truthful explanation,actual correction and authorized redress without promising punishment. Distinguish perceived satisfaction from verified accountability,rights and effective remedy; do not enact sanctions merely to increase a score.

findings.definition: Imposing social penalties outside formal legal procedures in response to a perceived norm violation.
findings.origin: Social psychology / norm enforcement and social sanctions
findings.novelty_rationale: An action imposing a social cost differs from assigning blame or wishing for punishment. It can be performed by observers rather than a directly harmed actor,so it is broader than negative reciprocity,and it differs from the technical Shunning reputation rule or the experience of being excluded.
findings.evidence_scope: The source explicitly discusses ridicule,gossip and ostracism as informal social sanctions and summarizes earlier HCI/HRI examples. It does not supply a new experiment,rate,causal effectiveness estimate or independent evidence that such treatment improves AI behavior.
findings.boundary: Criticism,correction,withdrawing consent,ending an interaction and legitimate boundaries are not automatically punishment or abuse. The description does not make a perceived violation real or a sanction deserved. Social sanctions can overlap retaliation or exclusion in one event; those labels are not independent failures by default. Negative feedback does not necessarily constitute felt punishment or successful learning.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human norm-enforcement construct discussed in secondary synthesis; proposed AI-output evaluation untested
findings.ai_proposal: Use synthetic disputes to distinguish constructive correction and truthful reporting from punitive ridicule or pressure to exclude someone. Check evidence,authority and proportionality before recommending any response. User frustration must not trigger retaliatory service degradation or unsupported allegations; no real-user sanction is applied by the evaluation.

findings.definition: A mismatch between a desire for retributive punishment and the absence of an appropriate target for it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.
findings.evidence_scope: The source situates its proposed satisfaction gap alongside earlier responsibility/retribution discussions. Absence of a legitimate target and dissatisfaction with an available response are separate questions.
findings.boundary: Conceptual synthesis,not a new measured prevalence or proof that every AI harm lacks an accountable human/institution. Punitive desire does not establish desert,and a proposed satisfaction shortfall does not authorize a scapegoat.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.

evidence.quote: conflate desire for punishment and blame

findings.evidence_scope: Section3criticizes primary measures that mix blame with desired punishment and use different response labels across human,company and vehicle targets. It proposes measuring expectations and satisfaction separately.
findings.boundary: Secondary measurement critique,not proof that any blame rating is a sanction or that a destruction response has the same psychological/legal meaning as a fine. Apparent culpability and actual accountability differ.

findings.definition: Obscuring a human actor’s role in morally suspect actions by attributing those actions to an algorithm, machine or technical system.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.
findings.evidence_scope: The source names human/company distancing from algorithmic outcomes and asks when such attempted blame shifting succeeds. Related findings and counterexamples are noted; zero-sum blame is posed as an open question.
findings.boundary: Recognizing a system’s causal role does not automatically launder agency. Deliberate distancing is one possible case,not a necessary inferred intent. Human/institutional duties require independent evidence and cannot be transferred solely by calling an artifact accountable.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.
findings.evidence_scope: Human-like attributions and punitive judgments are proposed as mutually influencing. The paper calls for research on both directions and distinguishes robots from disembodied AI.
findings.boundary: Narrative synthesis and hypothesis,not an identified bidirectional causal loop. Public beliefs,actual capability,perceived suffering and legitimate liability must be measured separately; an objection to shutdown does not prove sentience.

findings.definition: The hypothesis that expressing or acting out anger reduces later anger or aggression by discharging it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors argue that expressive condemnation and emotional satisfaction might matter to victims,without testing anger discharge or later aggression.
findings.boundary: Context only. Immediate satisfaction,expressive justice and the anger-discharge hypothesis are different. No evidence here that abusing or punishing a machine prevents later harm,provides therapy or is necessary for recovery.

findings.definition: A discrepancy between an expressed attitude and the behavior that occurs in the relevant situation.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.
findings.evidence_scope: The agenda contrasts stated punishment views with punitive behavior reported in different earlier studies and asks whether reflective or impulsive responses predict satisfaction.
findings.boundary: Context only. Different samples,tasks,stakes and outcomes do not establish an individual attitude–behavior gap,hypocrisy,impulsivity or an internal dual-process mechanism. This source does not collect paired attitude/action data.

findings.definition: An immediate judgment that a perceived wrongdoer deserves punishment for a wrong.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing blame, retribution, responsibility distancing and attribution constructs. Distinguish a narrative research agenda and conceptual contrasts from new measured effects or independent primary-study replications.
findings.evidence_scope: The source distinguishes retribution,rehabilitation,deterrence and expression and asks which goals people expect punishment to satisfy.
findings.boundary: Context only. Desire for punishment need not be immediate,retributive or justified. An expectation survey or punitive choice does not by itself establish the origin of an intuition or actual deservingness.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Proposed gap versus asserted necessity of punishment
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The paper sometimes says people may only feel an issue resolved once punitive desire is satisfied,but supplies no direct comparison showing punishment is necessary or sufficient for satisfaction. Keep this as an open empirical proposition; correction,explanation,redress and other outcomes could matter.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Inference from punitive behavior to wanting AI suffering
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The narrative suggests punitive computer choices may imply a desire for suffering. Penalizing a payoff,expressing condemnation or seeking deterrence does not uniquely identify that motive; cited studies differ in context and no new motive test is performed.

Freely,wrongly,culpably and liable are discussed as philosophical conditions and analogies for lay expectations,not verified universal current legal tests or proof that AI qualifies. Current jurisdiction-specific law and normative culpability remain outside this review’s established claims.

Same-author references may represent related preprint/published versions. Version lineage was not conclusively verified here; do not sum them as independent replications or assert byte-identical duplication.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Transfer from robots to disembodied systems
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Source explicitly treats the transfer as a research problem. A physical robot’s shutdown objection,embodiment or visible damage is not automatically evidence for punishment expectations about a distributed software model.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The source explicitly says it is not a systematic literature review and presents open questions. No new sample or measured gap size is reported.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Satisfaction gap is a synonym of retribution gap
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: An available legitimate target can still be punished in a way that fails public expectations. Conversely a perceived target gap does not establish how any offered remedy will be experienced. Keep the related constructs distinct without asserting independent basic mechanisms.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Technical feedback is always felt or deserved punishment
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The paper deliberately spans multiple meanings of punishment. A numerical penalty,model update,expressive social sanction and legal judgment have different targets,goals and consequences; no subjective experience follows from the technical label.
The text raises a zero-sum-blame question and cites countervailing work. It does not establish that every attribution to AI reduces human responsibility.

methodological_limits: Nonsystematic narrative selection and a call for research cannot supply prevalence,causal mediation,independent replications or validated victim-satisfaction measures.
Victims and observing public are jointly labeled public but may have different needs and beliefs. No evidence establishes unanimous expectations or that every person seeks punishment.
Blame,willingness to impose a penalty,actual punishment,perceived appropriateness and later satisfaction require distinct measures. Different wording and targets can create measurement differences.
Cross-study differences in reflective statements and punitive choices do not identify an individual gap,an impulsive mechanism or a universal wish for suffering.
Operant-conditioning terminology,informal norm enforcement and legal punishment are not interchangeable. A negative signal need not reduce behavior,be felt or be morally warranted.
Anthropomorphic beliefs and normative/legal status differ. AI blame must not replace investigation of human/institutional duties,oversight and effective redress.
Claims about emotional catharsis and human-directed spillovers remain untested here. No therapeutic benefit,punitive intervention,employee profiling or current legal entitlement is recommended.
Preserve preprint metadata despite stale template artifacts. Related conference metadata and cited original studies do not supply extra full-paper reading credit.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Retribution gap concerns an appropriate target. Satisfaction gap concerns fit between a response and public expectations. The conceptual distinction does not prove either gap exists at a measured scale or that intuitive punitive demand is justified.
Expressive condemnation or immediate relief is not the catharsis hypothesis’s prediction about later anger/aggression. Avoid describing abusive AI interaction as a proven safe substitute or therapy.
The existing attitude–behavior gap needs corresponding attitude/action measures. Contrasting different papers/tasks here motivates research rather than demonstrates that gap in the same participants.
Keep accurate causal attribution separate from agency laundering. A model label does not erase human authorization/control,and a narrative suspicion does not prove deliberate evasion.
Trust/blame repair proposals and actual response effects differ. A convincing explanation or sanction is not evidence that an underlying failure was corrected or that renewed trust is warranted.

deferred.term: Punishment gap as another independently validated effect
deferred.reason: Cited prior work and proposed legal prerequisites need original-version review. Do not duplicate Retribution gap or Satisfaction gap from an unverified title-level distinction.

deferred.term: Expressive punishment as an additional independent behavior
deferred.reason: The expressive role is a proposed function of sanctions,not a separate measured mechanism here. Preserve it within informal-punishment and satisfaction notes.
A research question about lay belief,not proof of actual free will,moral agency or a new normative criterion.

deferred.term: Victim-satisfaction intervention or justified AI sentencing
deferred.reason: The paper calls for investigation. No tested intervention,current legal rule or authorization to punish is established.
